sections.html:
Williamsport is the Lycoming County seat and the commercial center of north central Pennsylvania. About 27,384 people live in 11,320 households, and the population is down 1.3 percent from the 2020 base. Only 43.0 percent of housing units are owner-occupied. The midpoint home value is $154,300 and gross rent at the midpoint is $855.

Renters make up most households, so the buyer pool includes landlords and investors alongside families, and each group expects something different from a property. Hospital staff, instructors and plant workers value short drives and move-in-ready homes. Student renters keep demand steady for rental buildings.

sections.h2: Bureau of Codes fees and hours
sections.html:
The city's Bureau of Codes works from 200 Reighard Ave. It is open Monday to Friday from 8:00am to 4:00pm and closed for lunch from 12:00pm to 1:00pm. The main number is (570) 327-7517. Several lines in its fee schedule apply to owners who sell or rent.

Selected Bureau of Codes fees
Permit or inspectionFee
Rental property inspection$85 per building plus $15 for each additional unit
Rental re-inspection$30 per visit
Zoning occupancy permit$60
Zoning, building, fire occupancy$100
Certification of zoning and building$50 per request
College letter inspection$60 per address plus $15 per unit

Most permits issue within 15 business days of a completed application, except new construction or major reconstruction. Ask the Bureau which occupancy or certification letter your buyer or lender expects, and request it early.

sections.h2: Rental inspections and selling a landlord's building
sections.html:
A house with tenants, or one used as student housing, falls under the rental inspection fee schedule. A landlord selling a unit should find out whether the inspection is current and whether a re-inspection is still open.

  • Gather inspection reports and repair receipts for the buyer.
  • Check the unit count, because the fee grows with each unit in a building.
  • Sobriety houses, rooming houses and student residences have their own license line at $60 plus $15 per room, capped at $500.
  • Zoning matters for conversions. Variances and special exceptions each carry a $500 application fee, so confirm the legal use before you advertise a duplex or apartments.

A buyer paying cash for a tenant-occupied building can accept the inspection history as-is, but the closing agent will still want clean paperwork on each unit.

Water is the first thing buyers ask about. The West Branch Susquehanna River borders the city on the south. The March 1936 flood crested at 33.9 feet and reached High Street, and Hurricane Agnes in June 1972 set the wettest month on record at 16.80 inches. A flood control levee and the Susquehanna Riverwalk now run along the river.

Gather your flood insurance history, basement repair records and roof dates before you talk with a buyer. Those documents answer the questions that slow offers down. Photograph the basement, roofline and any river-side flood marks as well.

sections.h2: Transfer tax and recording in Lycoming County
sections.html:
Pennsylvania puts a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value transferred, and county recorders collect it along with any local tax. Both buyer and seller are jointly liable, and the contract decides who pays what. Some family transfers and transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

The Lycoming County Recorder of Deeds keeps land records back to 1795, with images online at the county's search portal. Williamsport is one of eleven school districts the county lists for transfer tax purposes, so the local share can be divided between the municipality and the school district. Ask the Recorder or your title company for the exact local rate and the current recording fee before closing.

To add or remove a name, a new deed must be drawn and recorded. A real estate attorney or title company can prepare it.

Several offices overlap here: the Bureau of Codes on Reighard Avenue, the county Recorder downtown and the title company handling settlement. A short checklist saves weeks.

  • Pull the parcel number and the names exactly as they appear on the deed.
  • Collect rental inspection letters, re-inspection results and any open permit paperwork.
  • Confirm the zoning use, particularly for duplexes, rooming houses and student residences.
  • Decide how you want to split the 1 percent state transfer tax and any local tax with the buyer.

With those items in a folder, you can compare a listing, a private sale and an as-is purchase on the same footing, and a buyer's questions get quick answers.

sections.h2: Does the city require an inspection when I sell?
sections.html:
Call the Bureau of Codes at (570) 327-7517 to ask which occupancy or certification letter applies to your property. A lender or buyer may request one, and the fee schedule lists the options. Rental properties carry a separate inspection fee, so say up front whether the house has tenants.

If the answer is that no letter is needed for an owner-occupied house, ask the Bureau to confirm that in writing or by email, so your title company and the buyer's lender are working from the same information. A request that comes in late can hold up a settlement date you have already promised.

Timing matters. Because most permits take up to 15 business days, ask for any letter as soon as you have a contract, then give your title company a copy for the closing file.

With renters in the majority, a Williamsport buyer may be a landlord who will price the building on its rent roll and inspection history rather than on how it looks. Have the unit count, current rents and lease end dates ready, along with proof that rental inspections are current. A building with open re-inspections or unclear zoning use sells slower and for less, so clear those items before you list if you can.

An owner-occupant buyer asks different questions: the roof, the heating system, the basement and the neighborhood. Keep receipts for recent work in one place, since a financed buyer's lender may want the same records.

sections.h2: What a sale looks like from contract to closing
sections.html:
After you accept an offer, the title company orders the payoff figures and drafts the deed, and you finish any letters the buyer or lender asked for. At settlement the deed is signed, the transfer tax and recording fee are paid, and the Recorder of Deeds files it. A cash buyer shortens the path because no appraisal or loan approval is involved.

If your building has tenants, tell them early when the buyer or an inspector will visit, and give the buyer the lease terms and inspection history for each unit.

faqs.q: Does the City of Williamsport require an inspection when I sell?
faqs.a: Ask the Bureau of Codes at (570) 327-7517, because the fee schedule lists occupancy and certification letters that a lender or buyer may request. Rental properties have a separate inspection fee of $85 per building plus $15 per added unit.

faqs.q: How much is a rental inspection in Williamsport?
faqs.a: A rental property inspection costs $85 per building plus $15 for each additional unit in the building. A re-inspection visit costs $30.

faqs.q: Who records the deed on a Williamsport sale?
faqs.a: The Lycoming County Recorder of Deeds. Pennsylvania's 1 percent state realty transfer tax is collected there with any local tax and the recording fee, and the deed is not recorded until payment is made.

faqs.q: Does flooding affect selling in Williamsport?
faqs.a: It can. The city borders the West Branch Susquehanna River and has a flood history, including a 33.9 foot crest in 1936. Have your insurance and repair records ready, because buyers will ask.

faqs.q: How long does a permit take in Williamsport?
faqs.a: Most permits are issued within 15 business days of submitting the required application. New construction and major reconstruction can take longer.
